items.q: What is trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) and how does it treat gastric cancer?
items.a: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd, brand name Enhertu) is an antibody-drug conjugate that combines the HER2-targeting trastuzumab antibody with a potent topoisomerase I inhibitor payload called deruxtecan, delivering chemotherapy directly into HER2-positive gastric cancer cells while limiting damage to healthy tissue. The drug carries a high drug-to-antibody ratio of eight DXd molecules per antibody, and its bystander effect allows it to also kill neighbouring HER2-negative cells, extending activity across tumours with mixed HER2 expression. Whether T-DXd is the right option depends on HER2 testing results, prior treatment, and review by a qualified oncology team.

items.q: How is T-DXd different from older HER2-targeted drugs like trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1)?
items.a: T-DXd differs from older HER2 antibody-drug conjugates mainly in its drug-to-antibody ratio and payload design — it carries eight cytotoxic DXd molecules per antibody, more than double T-DM1's ratio of about 3.5, producing a higher intracellular drug concentration once the antibody binds and is internalised by HER2-positive cells. T-DXd's payload also crosses cell membranes to kill nearby HER2-negative tumour cells through a 'bystander effect,' which may explain its activity in tumours with heterogeneous HER2 expression. This mechanism does not guarantee response in every patient, and use should be guided by a treating oncology team.

items.q: Who is eligible for T-DXd treatment in HER2-positive gastric cancer?
items.a: T-DXd is generally considered for gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer patients with HER2 IHC 3+ or IHC 2+ tumours who have already progressed on a trastuzumab-containing regimen, have adequate organ function, and have no active lung disease, based on the eligibility criteria used in the DESTINY-Gastric01 trial's ECOG performance status 0–1 population. Because active interstitial lung disease is a contraindication, lung function is assessed before starting treatment. Actual eligibility depends on cancer type, stage, biomarker profile (HER2 status), prior treatment, and specialist review, and should be discussed with a qualified oncology team.

items.q: How effective is T-DXd for HER2-positive gastric cancer, based on clinical trial results?
items.a: In the DESTINY-Gastric01 trial, second-line T-DXd produced a 51.3% objective response rate versus 14.3% with chemotherapy, and extended median overall survival to 12.5 months versus 8.4 months, corresponding to roughly a 41% reduction in the hazard of death. In the DESTINY-Gastric02 trial conducted in Western patients, T-DXd showed a confirmed response rate of 41.8% and median overall survival of 12.1 months. These results come from clinical trial populations, and individual outcomes vary depending on cancer stage, prior treatment, and overall health — final expectations should be discussed with the treating oncology team.

items.q: Can T-DXd be used as a first-line treatment before trastuzumab?
items.a: T-DXd is not currently approved as a first-line treatment for HER2-positive gastric cancer; it is approved for use after prior trastuzumab-containing therapy has stopped working, with trastuzumab plus chemotherapy (sometimes combined with nivolumab) remaining the standard first-line approach. Trials evaluating T-DXd earlier in treatment, including DESTINY-Gastric05, are ongoing but have not yet changed first-line standards. Whether an alternative sequencing may be considered depends on cancer stage, prior treatment, biomarker profile, and specialist review, and should be discussed with a qualified oncology team.

items.q: What are the most common side effects of T-DXd treatment?
items.a: The most common T-DXd side effects are nausea, reported in about 74% of patients, and fatigue, reported in about 59%, with most cases graded mild to moderate and manageable with antiemetic prophylaxis and supportive care rather than requiring treatment discontinuation. Hair loss occurs in roughly 30% of patients, and blood count changes such as neutropenia, anaemia, and thrombocytopenia occur at rates comparable to standard chemotherapy. Side effect severity and management vary by individual, and any new or worsening symptoms should be reported promptly to the treating oncology team.

items.q: What is the risk of interstitial lung disease (ILD) with T-DXd, and how is it monitored?
items.a: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is the most serious known risk of T-DXd, occurring in an estimated 10–15% of patients in the DESTINY gastric trials at any grade, with severe grade 3–4 ILD in about 1–3%, which is why active monitoring is built into every treatment cycle. Monitoring typically includes a baseline chest CT before the first dose, symptom checks for new cough, breathlessness, or fever at every visit, and prompt chest imaging if symptoms appear. Depending on ILD grade, T-DXd may be paused, treated with corticosteroids, or permanently discontinued — decisions that rest with the treating oncology team.

items.q: Can I receive T-DXd if my gastric cancer is HER2 IHC 2+ but ISH testing was not done?
items.a: T-DXd eligibility criteria in several markets, including China's NMPA approval, cover HER2 IHC 3+ and IHC 2+ results without always requiring separate ISH confirmation, unlike trastuzumab, which generally needs ISH confirmation for IHC 2+ cases. This is thought to relate to T-DXd's bystander effect, which maintains activity across a broader range of HER2 expression. Because testing requirements vary by country and treating institution, whether T-DXd may be considered for a specific IHC result depends on the treating centre's own criteria and specialist review.

items.q: How much does T-DXd (Enhertu) treatment cost for gastric cancer?
items.a: T-DXd treatment cost is not fixed and is typically estimated on a per-cycle or per-course basis, varying by country, hospital, number of cycles administered, and whether ILD monitoring such as chest CT scans or hospitalisation is required during treatment. Because T-DXd is a biologic ADC administered by infusion at intervals guided by response and tolerability, an accurate estimate requires review of HER2 status, treatment history, and the chosen treatment centre. Actual costs should be confirmed directly with the treating hospital and discussed with a qualified oncology team before treatment begins.

items.q: Is T-DXd available in China for gastric cancer treatment, and how can CancerFax help access it?
items.a: Yes, T-DXd (Enhertu) has NMPA approval in China for HER2-positive gastric cancer and is available at major academic cancer centres, with RC48 (disitamab vedotin), a Chinese-developed HER2 antibody-drug conjugate, available as an additional option. CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or trials, estimate costs, and coordinate travel, visa, and follow-up support alongside the treating oncology team. Final treatment decisions, including centre selection and treatment sequencing, remain with the treating medical team.
